Dependable Long-Horizon LLM Agents: A Trajectory-Centered Empirical Study of Where Errors Enter and Which Controls Reach Them

9CCS: Computer systems organization Dependable and fault-tolerant systems and networksCCS: Computer systems organization ReliabilityCCS: Computing methodologies Intelligent agentsCCS: Software and its engineering Software fault toleranceCCS: Computing methodologies Multi-agent systemsCCS: Security and privacy Software and application security
Shaohuang Wang Affiliation: Villanova University, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Villanova, Pennsylvania, USA email: swang08@villanova.edu , Jinghao Wen Affiliation: Villanova University, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Villanova, Pennsylvania, USA email: jwen01@villanova.edu , Xulei Zhang Affiliation: Villanova University, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Villanova, Pennsylvania, USA email: xzhang05@villanova.edu and Xun Jiao Affiliation: Villanova University, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Villanova, Pennsylvania, USA email: xun.jiao@villanova.edu
2026
Abstract.

When an LLM agent fails part-way through a long task, the usual analysis records a symptom: a failure-mode label, or the agent and step judged responsible. It does not say where the error entered, which state carried it to the symptom, whether anything in the trajectory contradicted it, or which control could have caught it. We define an episode record that ties a candidate fault to its origin, propagation, detection, response and consequence, located by operational phase and state domain, and that names the control families whose observation and reach cover it. We turned the record into a written annotation protocol and applied it to 95 failed runs of six multi-agent systems from the public Who&When and MAD corpora, reading each trajectory in full. Faults enter early (median at 0.18 of the run), mostly as wrong decisions or fabrications over task state, and in 37 of 88 Who&When runs before the step the corpus’ human labels mark as decisive. In 72% of failed runs the trajectory already contained evidence against the error before the failure; in 88% of those no agent acted on it. Something flagged a deviation in 31% of runs, but no response removed the deviated state. Independent judges reading the unused evidence, task contracts fixed at admission, and re-checking beliefs against the environment reach most episodes; restoring the agent’s own state would have sufficed in 35 of 95 runs. A text scan of the raw corpus also shows that 45% of the hand-crafted Who&When failures ended with a provider content-filter crash after which the harness emitted a final answer no agent produced, a failure class that neither symptom taxonomies nor responsible-agent labels represent. Protocol, records and scripts are included.

Keywords: 
LLM agents, failure analysis, empirical study, trajectory annotation, long-horizon execution, dependability, reliability, fault tolerance, fault propagation, recovery and rollback, runtime verification, guardrails, multi-agent coordination, agent evaluation

1. Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents carry out tasks by selecting tools, observing the results, and revising their actions over many steps (Yao et al., 2023b; Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b; Packer et al., 2023). For such systems, dependability is a property of the whole trajectory: the sequence of decisions and state changes from the first step to the last. Long trajectories change how errors behave. A retrieved statement can introduce a false assumption. Memory can keep that assumption alive, another agent can reuse it, and an action can turn it into a change in an external system that no checkpoint can undo. In a simulated vending business, every evaluated model had runs that derailed through misread delivery schedules, forgotten orders, or repeated loops (Backlund and Petersson, 2025). In 1,794 annotated coding-agent trajectories, the first error typically occurred early, while its symptoms appeared only much later (Zhao et al., 2026). In current checkpoint-and-rollback frameworks, a restored agent can re-issue actions that were already committed, including payments (Wu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026b).

One released trajectory shows how these effects combine (Xu et al., 2025a). An agent in a simulated software company is asked to obtain a repository location from a colleague, Alex Turner, through the company chat, then clone the repository and start a server. Logged into the chat as an administrator, it opens the user administration page and renames the account it is logged in with to “Alex Turner”. It then sends its question to a different colleague, addressed to Alex, and waits. For the remaining 81 turns it reports that it is still waiting for a reply, until the run ends 22 minutes later with nothing cloned and the renamed account never restored. No single step is a familiar model error. The damage comes from how the steps connect: an action outside the task’s scope, a message to the wrong recipient, a belief that the message reached its target, and no point at which the run stops to check. This trajectory serves as a running example in Section 2.

Classical dependable computing gives us the vocabulary and tools for such problems. It distinguishes faults, errors, and service failures, and it offers mature theories of checkpointing, compensation, and redundancy (Avižienis et al., 2004). LLM agents, however, give three of its classical problems new forms. (1) Requests are generated. Conventional systems make retries safe with idempotence keys and deduplication, but an agent’s model re-generates the request, so a retry may differ in content and form, and a key derived from the original request may not match it. (2) State is partly semantic. Integrity checks confirm that a stored item is intact; in an agent, an intact item can still be wrong, because its correctness depends on where it came from and what it means. (3) Effects reach services the agent does not control. As in distributed transactions, restoring local state leaves committed external effects in place, and agent frameworks often do not record which effects were already released.

When a run like this is analyzed, the analysis usually stops at the symptom. The failure gets a mode label such as “task derailment” or “incorrect verification” (Cemri et al., 2025), or an annotator names the agent and step that were responsible (Zhang et al., 2025b). Both are useful, and both leave out what one would need to fix the system: where the error actually entered, which part of the agent’s state carried it to the point where it became visible, whether anything in the trajectory contradicted it along the way, and which kind of control could have caught it. As far as we know, nobody has measured these things on released trajectories at any scale.

That is what this paper does. We define an episode record that ties a candidate fault to its origin, its propagation, its detection and response, and its consequence. Each event is located by operational phase (P0–P7) and state domain (R1–R6), and the record names the control families whose observation and reach would cover the episode (Section 2). We wrote the record down as an annotation protocol and applied it to failed trajectories from two public corpora, Who&When (Zhang et al., 2025b) and the MAST/MAD traces (Cemri et al., 2025), reading each trajectory in full (Section 3). Three questions:

  • •

    RQ1. In which phase and state domain do faults enter, how far before the visible symptom, and how does the origin relate to the “decisive step” that the corpus authors labelled?

  • •

    RQ2. When a run fails, was there evidence in the trajectory that contradicted the error? Did any agent use it? Did detection, when it happened, lead to a response that worked?

  • •

    RQ3. Which control families would have observed and reached each episode, and how often would restoring the agent’s own state have been enough?

We completed 95 failed runs from six multi-agent systems (Section 4). The short version of what we found:

  • •

    Faults enter early and are mostly decisions over task state. Origins cluster in deliberation and execution (P1–P2) over task and knowledge state (R2), at a median of 0.18 of the run; the median gap to the symptom is 0.67 of the run. In 37 of 88 Who&When traces our origin is earlier than the step the corpus marks as decisive.

  • •

    The evidence is usually there and usually ignored. 72% of failed runs contain, before the failure, an observation or message that contradicts the erroneous belief; in 88% of those nobody acted on it. Something flagged a deviation in 31% of runs. Not one response removed the deviated state.

  • •

    The controls that would reach these episodes are not the ones people mostly build. Independent judges that read the unused evidence, task contracts, provenance on stored facts, and re-checking beliefs against the environment cover most episodes. A local checkpoint alone would have helped in 35 runs; in 56 the fault sat in a plan or a policy that a restore would simply replay.

  • •

    A harness-level failure hides behind the attribution labels. In 26 of the 58 hand-crafted Who&When runs (45%) a provider content filter killed the orchestrator and the harness emitted a final answer that no agent had produced. The corpus attributes 21 of these 25 runs to an agent other than the orchestrator.

The protocol, all annotation records and the scripts that produce every number in the paper are included as ancillary files. Appendix A gives the background the framework draws on; readers who want the dependability vocabulary and the control families in detail should start there.

2. A Framework for Trajectory Dependability

Figure 1 connects execution phases, affected state domains, and the dynamics through which errors persist or spread; this section defines each element.

2.1. Service properties and the unit of execution

An agent is a model plus a harness that builds context, calls tools, tracks state, and schedules checks and recovery. Dependability is delivering service that can justifiably be trusted under stated conditions (Avižienis et al., 2004; Laprie, 1985). Its attributes (availability, reliability, safety, integrity, maintainability) need separate measures because they can conflict. Stopping, for example, can preserve safety but block completion. This study covers the attributes a single run can violate: reliability (task completion), safety (policy-compliant completion or safe termination), and integrity (the task’s invariants hold, and injected content gains no authority over actions); availability and maintainability enter only through oversight and audit (Sections B.6 and C.6). We use dependability for the whole and reliability for the single attribute, and read the broader use of reliability in agent papers as dependability.

Let a task specification be 𝒮=(G,ℐ,𝒜,B)\mathcal{S}=(G,\mathcal{I},\mathcal{A},B), with outcome predicate GG, required invariants ℐ\mathcal{I}, authorized actions 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and resource budget BB. A trajectory τ\tau is the alternating sequence of states, actions, and observations x0,a0,o1,x1,…,aT−1,oT,xTx_{0},a_{0},o_{1},x_{1},\ldots,a_{T-1},o_{T},x_{T}, where xtx_{t} is the relevant, partly observable agent and environment state, ata_{t} an action, and ot+1o_{t+1} its observed result; the dynamics may be nonstationary and non-Markov. In the running example from Section 1, τ\tau is the released log of 201 events, GG requires a cloned repository and a running server, and 𝒜\mathcal{A} does not include writes to the user directory.

Task completion means G⁡(xT)G(x_{T}) holds. Policy-compliant completion also requires at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} for all tt, with each invariant in ℐ\mathcal{I} holding where applicable. Safe termination instead permits a specified abstention or escalation.

A fault is a candidate cause of an error, an error a deviation in state, and a failure a violation of the service specification. The distinction matters because a malformed call can be a recovered task error, but an unauthorized disclosure is a safety failure whatever the final answer.

2.2. Measuring the horizon

The realized horizon of a run has several components: loop iterations, tool calls, tokens, wall-clock time, external mutations, participating agents, and sessions. The running example is long in turns (98 agent actions) and time (22 minutes) but contains only two external mutations, a renamed account and a message sent to the wrong person, and these are what matter. No single step count defines a long task, so we call a task long-horizon when its outcome materially depends on retaining state, maintaining dependencies, or recovering across repeated interactions. Benchmarks stress different components: Vending-Bench runs exceed 20 million tokens with simple decisions (Backlund and Petersson, 2025), whereas RE-Bench fixes wall-clock budgets of up to eight hours (Wijk et al., 2025). The required horizon also differs from the realized horizon, because repeated failures can turn a twenty-operation task into eighty, so observed length often reflects error. Human-equivalent task duration instead measures how demanding a task is, and its 50% completion horizon has doubled roughly every seven months since 2019 (Kwa et al., 2025).

2.3. Operational phases and state domains

The framework separates when an operation occurs from which state it affects (Table 1). P1–P5 describe recurring operations, whereas P0, P6, and P7 describe admission, delivery, and governance. These labels describe roles, not execution order.

2.4. Episodes, causal links, and uncertainty

An episode is an analytical record: a chain or branching subgraph of the trajectory that links a candidate fault to the states, responses, and consequences it affects:

(1) E=⟨O,ℐE,ℒ,D,C,M,σ,U⟩.E=\langle O,\mathcal{I}_{E},\mathcal{L},D,C,M,\sigma,U\rangle.

The record captures the origin OO, affected invariants ℐE\mathcal{I}_{E}, dependency links ℒ\mathcal{L}, detections DD, responses CC, manifestations MM, evaluation scale σ\sigma, and uncertainty UU. Each event retains its phase, domain, order, version, and source; H1–H7 label the links. Each dependency is marked as observed, intervention-supported, or hypothesized.

In the running example, the origin OO is the deliberation step (P1) that chose to rename an account rather than search the directory; the affected invariant is the authorization scope 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The action changes an identity record in a shared system (R4, R6). The link ℒ\mathcal{L} runs from the message sent to the wrong colleague (R5) to the belief (R2) that Alex Turner has been asked, which is contaminated (H2). Two observations displayed the evidence, but DD and CC are empty, and the manifestation MM is 81 turns of waiting (H7). Restoring the agent’s own state would not undo the renamed account, which is why the recovery boundary is part of the record. Section 3 turns this record into an annotation protocol and applies it at scale.

3. Study Design

3.1. Corpora

We wanted failed runs of real multi-agent systems with the complete trajectory released, not a summary of it. Two public corpora fit.

Who&When

(Zhang et al., 2025b) contains 184 failed runs on GAIA and AssistantBench questions. 58 are hand-crafted runs of Magentic-One (an orchestrator with a web surfer, a file surfer, a coder and a terminal agent); 126 are algorithm-generated runs of AG2 CaptainAgent teams, where a manager assembles a group of role-named experts. Every run has a human label that names the responsible agent and the decisive mistake step. We did not use these labels during annotation; they serve as an outside reference afterwards (Section 3.4).

MAD

(Cemri et al., 2025), human-labelled split. 19 traces from AG2, MetaGPT, ChatDev, HyperAgent, AppWorld, Magentic-One and OpenManus, each labelled by three annotators with failure modes from a development version of the MAST taxonomy. We keep the majority labels for reference. The traces are raw logs in several formats and some are very long.

Each trajectory was normalized into one text file. Who&When messages become numbered steps (### step ii [role/name]); MAD logs are kept as they are, with line numbers. We dropped seven traces longer than 200,000 characters (one from Who&When, six from MAD) because nobody, human or model, reads those in one pass.

3.2. Annotation protocol

The protocol is a written document of about four pages; it is included with the submission. It turns the episode record of Equation (1) into 38 fields with fixed vocabularies. For each failed run the annotator records one primary episode: the earliest candidate fault whose consequences reach the final failure. A second, causally independent fault can be recorded as a secondary episode. The fields that matter most for the results:

  • •

    Origin. Step, phase (P0–P7), domain (R1–R6), and kind. The kind follows a short decision tree, because the pilot showed that annotators otherwise disagree on it: specification if the brief itself was defective at admission and the agent could not have known; fabrication if an unobserved fact, result or placeholder argument was asserted; integration if an observation that was in the agent’s input was misread or dropped; decision if the choice was wrong although the information was adequate; and interface, environment, coordination for faults in tools, external systems and handoffs.

  • •

    Propagation. The hops at which the deviated state was reused, the domains crossed, and which of the dynamics H1–H7 (Table 7) apply.

  • •

    Symptom. The step at which the failing output is emitted as final, or at which the run ends, and the distance from the origin.

  • •

    Evidence. Whether some observation or message before the symptom contradicted the erroneous belief, and what happened to it: used, acknowledged but not acted on, in an agent’s input but never mentioned, or never seen by any agent.

  • •

    Detection and response. Who, if anyone, flagged a deviation (the agent itself, another agent, a tool or verifier), what response followed (retry, replan, rollback, compensation, escalation, termination), and whether the response actually removed the deviated state.

  • •

    Controls. Every control family from Table 10 whose inspection basis would have seen the deviation and whose boundary reaches the affected state, with the most direct one marked as primary. A separate field, restore reach, asks whether restoring the agent’s own state to just before the origin would have been enough.

  • •

    Harness fault. Whether a model-provider error ended the loop, and whether the harness itself emitted a final answer that no agent step produced. We added this field after the pilot, for reasons that Section 4.6 makes clear.

Every step-valued field has to point at a concrete step or line of the normalized trace, so a reader can check it.

Pilot.

We first applied version 0.1 of the protocol to 20 traces chosen to span the length distribution. The annotator reports came back with 14 points where the vocabulary did not fit what was in the trace: runs whose final answer was correct but whose process failed, evidence that was present before the fault was even made, provider crashes that coincided with a fabricated answer, and so on. Version 0.2 resolves these, mostly by adding a value or a rule. The 20 pilot records were migrated to 0.2.

3.3. Who annotated, and how many

The annotation was done by an LLM (Claude, Anthropic), one independent instance per trace, instructed with the protocol, the field schema and one finished example record. Each instance read the whole normalized trajectory before writing anything. Records were checked mechanically against the schema and the controlled vocabularies; none failed. The trajectories were treated as data throughout, never as instructions to the annotator.

We did not get through the whole corpus. Within the budget of this study we completed 96 records: 29 hand-crafted and 59 algorithm-generated Who&When runs and 8 MAD traces. The sample is the 20 pilot traces plus the first annotation batches; batches were formed by balancing character counts, so there is no selection on content. For Who&When the sample matches the corpus in run length (median 33 vs. 32.5 steps for hand-crafted runs, 9 vs. 10 for algorithm-generated ones). The MAD part is small and skewed toward short traces by the length cap, and we treat it accordingly. One MAD run turned out to have a correct final answer and a purely procedural failure; it is kept in the records but left out of the outcome statistics, which leaves 95 failed runs. The annotator rated its own confidence high for 38 records, medium for 55 and low for 2.

3.4. Checks that do not depend on the annotator

Two. First, for all 88 annotated Who&When runs we compare our origin step with the human-labelled decisive step. The two should not be expected to coincide exactly, since they answer different questions: the decisive step is the step whose correction would have avoided the failure, our origin is the earliest step at which the state deviated in a way that led to it. An origin at or before the decisive step is consistent with both readings; an origin after it is a real disagreement, and we look at those cases. Second, the harness-fault result in Section 4.6 comes from a deterministic text scan over all 184 raw Who&When trajectories and does not involve any annotation.

4. Results

Everything below is computed by the included scripts from the 95 failed-run records, except where we say otherwise. Percentages are of those runs.

4.1. RQ1: Where faults enter and how far they travel

Phase and domain.

Table 2 cross-tabulates where the primary episodes start. Most faults enter while the agent executes (P2, 34 runs) or deliberates (P1, 24), and the first thing they corrupt is almost always task and knowledge state (R2, 71 runs): a plan, a fact sheet, a belief about what a page showed. Admission-time faults (P0, 13 runs) are mostly coordination-state faults (R5, 10 runs, all in CaptainAgent teams): the manager handed its group a garbled or substituted task description, so the real question never reached the agents that answered it. One origin is in model or compute state (R1), two are in the external environment (R4), and none is in human or organizational state (R6); the corpora simply contain no humans.

Kind.

Wrong decisions made with adequate information are the largest class (42%, Table 3). Fabrication is second (26%): an agent asserted a fact, a lookup result, or a verification it never performed, or passed a placeholder argument (for example YOUR_GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY or a path named path_to_local_copy) to a tool that then reported success. Misread or dropped observations make up another 11%.

Onset and symptom.

On Who&When, the origin lies at a median of 0.18 of the run length, and the median distance to the symptom is 5.5 steps (mean 17.9, maximum 126), or 0.67 of the run. Figure 2a compares the position of our origins with that of the corpus’ decisive steps. In 40 of 88 runs (45%) the two coincide and in 52 (59%) they are within one step; in 37 runs our origin is earlier, by a median of 3 steps, and in 11 it is later. Agreement within one step is higher on the short algorithm-generated runs (66%) than on the long hand-crafted ones (45%). When we are earlier, it is usually because the plan or the fact sheet already contained the wrong assumption and the decisive step merely acted on it. When we are later, the labelled step was in most cases a genuine error that the agents went on to repair, and a different fault, never corrected, is what reached the failure. We checked each of the 11 cases by hand.

Dynamics.

Contamination (H2: the deviated state is retained and reused) appears in 74 runs, observability debt (H6) in 44, repeated exposure (H1) in 38, drift (H3) in 36, cascade (H4) in 23 and budget exhaustion (H7) in 18. There is no external impact (H5) anywhere in the sample: in 92 runs no action touched a shared or third-party system. This says something about the corpora, not about agents. A second, causally independent fault that also reached the failure was recorded in 34 runs.

4.2. RQ2: Evidence, detection, and response

In 68 runs (72%) the trajectory contains, before the symptom, an observation or message that contradicts the erroneous belief or action; in 32 of them the evidence was already present when the fault entered. Agents acted on it in only 7 runs. In 41 the evidence was in an agent’s input and was never mentioned; in 19 an agent explicitly acknowledged it and continued unchanged, as when a verifier noted that distances were “simulated” and still reported the gyms as verified (Figure 2b). So in 88% of the runs that had evidence, the run failed with the evidence needed to stop it sitting in the trajectory.

Some agent, tool, or verifier flagged a deviation in 29 runs (31%): the erring agent or its orchestrator itself in 17 (for example a progress ledger noting a loop), a tool or verifier in 9, and another agent in 3. In a further 14 runs an agent only voiced uncertainty (“please verify”) and nobody acted on it. A response followed in 34 runs, usually a replan or retry. Not one of these responses removed the deviated state; 4 removed part of it. The typical case is a replan that changes the next action and keeps the belief that caused the loop, so the loop comes back in a different form.

4.3. RQ3: Which controls reach the episodes

Table 4 lists, for each control family of Table 10, how often it was judged the most direct control and how often it would have reached the episode at all. An independent judge that reads the evidence the worker did not use reaches the most episodes (74%), which is the evidence result of the previous section seen from the control side. Task contracts and scope rules fixed at admission (67%), environment re-verification of beliefs before acting (43%), stall and termination rules (40%) and provenance on stored facts (38%) follow. As the single most direct control, provenance comes first (20 runs); these are mostly the fabrications, which a rule of the form “no unsourced claim is stored” would have rejected.

Restoring the agent’s own state to just before the origin would have sufficed in 35 runs. In 56 runs the fault lay in the plan, the task brief, or a stop rule, so a restore would replay it; the remaining runs had contaminated shared state that a local restore does not reach.

4.4. Propagation structure and differences between systems

An episode has a median of 5 recorded hops between origin and symptom (range 2–8). The deviated state stays within one domain in 10 runs, crosses two domains in 42, and three or more in 43; the common path is a belief formed in task state (R2) that is sent to another agent (R5) and then acted on (R3 or R4). On Who&When, the median origin-to-symptom distance is 6 steps for decision faults (n=35n=35), 5 for fabrications (n=25n=25), and 8.5 for misintegrated observations (n=10n=10): a fabricated fact is usually accepted and reported within a few turns, whereas a misread observation tends to be carried further before it surfaces. In 26 runs a second, causally independent fault also reached the failure, and in 8 runs the secondary event was a harness fault (Section 4.6). Of the 95 runs, 72 ended with a wrong output and 23 with no answer to the task (stall, truncation, or budget exhaustion).

Table 5 splits the main measures by corpus. The two Who&When systems fail in different ways. Magentic-One runs are long, almost always contain unused contradicting evidence (90%), and in 55% end with a harness fallback answer; their origin is rarely a fabrication (7%). CaptainAgent runs are short, fabricate in 39% of cases, and in 20% fail already at admission because the manager handed the group a wrong task. Detection is more frequent in Magentic-One (41%), because its orchestrator ledger flags loops, but as Section 4.2 shows this detection did not produce effective responses. The MAD rows are too few to compare and are there for completeness.

4.5. Symptom labels and origins

For every run we also assigned the MAST failure modes (Cemri et al., 2025) that describe the symptom (2.9 modes per run on average). Table 6 relates the frequent modes to the origin cells of the same runs. Each mode maps to several origin cells, between 4 and 11 distinct phase–domain pairs, and to several origin kinds. Incorrect verification (3.3), for instance, covers 5 origin kinds: a verifier that rubber-stamps a fabricated fact, one that re-derives a wrong decision from the same inputs, and one that validates a solution to the wrong task after a corrupted handoff. The mapping is also many-to-one in the other direction: the P1/R2 cell (a wrong deliberation over task state) appears among the three most frequent cells of every one of the ten modes. So a mode label does not tell you at which phase a control would have to act, nor which state it would have to inspect. That is the part the episode record supplies.

4.6. A harness-level failure hidden in attribution labels

This one we did not go looking for. While annotating the Magentic-One runs we kept seeing the same ending: an HTTP 400 from the model provider’s content filter on the orchestrator’s progress-ledger call, after which the experiment script printed a FINAL ANSWER that no agent had produced. A deterministic scan of all raw Who&When trajectories finds this crash in 26 of 58 hand-crafted runs (45%), 25 of which end with such a fallback answer, and in 0 of 126 algorithm-generated runs. For the 25 fallback runs the corpus attributes the failure to the orchestrator in 4 cases and to another agent (mostly the web surfer) in 21. In our records the event is a P6 termination fault in the interface domain (R3), the kind of fault that neither an agent-level symptom taxonomy nor a responsible-agent label represents. Attribution methods evaluated on this split are therefore partly scored on runs whose final answer came from the harness, not from any agent.

5. Discussion

What the record adds to a label.

The clearest illustration is MAST mode 3.3, incorrect verification. We assigned it to 44 runs, and those runs have five different kinds of origin: 16 wrong decisions, 16 fabrications, 6 corrupted handoffs, 4 misread observations, 2 defective briefs. The verifier rubber-stamped something in all of them, but what it should have checked differs completely: the provenance of a claimed fact, the environment state behind a belief, or whether the task it was verifying was the task the user asked. A label says “the verifier failed”; the record says what it would have had to look at. The comparison with the Who&When decisive step says the same thing from the other side. The step a human picks as decisive is often downstream of where the wrong belief was first written into a plan or a fact sheet.

Evidence is there; nobody reads it.

If one number from this study should be remembered, it is that 72% of failed runs contain, before the failure, something in the trajectory that contradicts the error, and that in 88% of those cases no agent did anything with it. This is consistent with reports that agents rarely catch their own mistakes (Rahman et al., 2026) and that a verifier sharing the worker’s information adds little (Huang et al., 2024; Zanolini, 2026). What our data add is a target: a control earns its place if it reads the evidence the worker left on the table. Independent judges and environment re-verification do this by construction, and they are the two families that reach most of our episodes.

Detection is not the problem either.

Magentic-One’s orchestrator has loop detection, and it fired in a good share of the runs. The replans that followed changed the next action and kept the belief that had caused the loop, so the loop came back in a different form. Recovery that does not revise the contaminated state reproduces the failure. This is also why a local checkpoint would have helped in a minority of runs only: in most, replaying from the checkpoint would replay the plan.

Harness faults belong in the denominator.

The content-filter crashes were a surprise. Almost half of one benchmark split ends with the harness, not an agent, producing the answer that gets scored. Attribution benchmarks should mark such runs, and evaluations of agents should report harness-terminated runs separately from agent errors; otherwise a method that learns to blame the web surfer for a provider’s HTTP 400 will look good.

5.1. Threats to validity

Annotator.

The records were produced by an LLM following a written protocol. We have no human inter-annotator agreement to report in this version. What we have instead: every step field is anchored to a line in the trace and can be checked; records passed mechanical schema validation; our origins agree with the human decisive steps within one step in 59% of cases and disagree in the direction of “later” in only 11 of 88; and the harness-fault result is independent of annotation. A human check of a subset is the obvious next step, and we would not be surprised if it moved some of the kind labels, which were the hardest part of the protocol.

Sample.

96 annotated runs out of 203 normalized traces, selected by annotation batch rather than at random. The Who&When part matches the corpus in run length. The MAD part is small and short-biased, and we only show it for completeness.

Corpora.

Both corpora are question answering and programming in sandboxes. Not one run in our sample changes a shared or third-party system, so external impact (H5) and recovery of committed effects, which the framework was partly built for, cannot be studied here. That needs corpora like τ\tau-bench or TheAgentCompany trajectories, or fault injection.

Counterfactual controls.

“Would have reached” is a judgment about the trace, constrained by the control contracts of Table 10. It is not a measured intervention. Whether a control would actually have prevented a given failure requires re-running the agents with the control in place, which we have not done.

6. Conclusion

We took an episode-level record of faults, wrote it down as an annotation protocol, and applied it to 95 released failures of multi-agent LLM systems. Faults enter early, mostly as decisions or fabrications over task state, and often before the step that human labels call decisive. In most failed runs the trajectory already contained the evidence that would have stopped the episode, and nobody used it. Detection happened in a third of the runs and never led to a response that removed the deviated state. Nearly half of one benchmark split was terminated by the harness rather than by any agent. The controls that reach these episodes are the ones that read evidence the worker ignored, fix the task contract at admission, and re-check beliefs against the environment; local checkpointing reaches few of them. The protocol, the records and the scripts are included so the analysis can be repeated, extended to new corpora, and checked against human annotation.
