Appendix A Background: Dynamics, Controls, and Published Evidence

The appendices below give the background the episode framework rests on: the long-horizon dynamics it encodes (Appendix B), the control families and their contracts used in Table 4 (Appendix C), evaluation practice (Appendix D), and a synthesis of published evidence (Appendix E).

Appendix B Challenges and Long-Horizon Dynamics

Because each decision in agent execution carries state and consequences forward, six challenges arise. Sections B.1–B.2 examine dependent errors and persistent state, Sections B.3–B.4 actions and incomplete verification, and Sections B.5–B.6 coordination and oversight, while Section B.7 consolidates them into seven dynamics.

B.1. Repeated execution and dependent errors

This subsection asks how the chance of failure changes as a run gets longer and after an error has occurred. A familiar illustration assumes NN necessary steps, each independently correct with probability pp:

(2) Pr⁡(all steps correct)=pN.\Pr(\text{all steps correct})=p^{N}.

At p=.99p=.99, this probability falls below one half at 69 steps. This is only a baseline, because recovery allows success after an error and dependence can push joint correctness well above or below pNp^{N}. For an absorbing service-failure event FF, the chain rule gives the general form

(3) SN=Pr⁡(F​ absent by ​N)=∏t=1N(1−λt),λt=Pr⁡(F​ first occurs at ​t∣F​ absent before ​t),S_{N}=\Pr(F\text{ absent by }N)=\prod_{t=1}^{N}(1-\lambda_{t}),\qquad\lambda_{t}=\Pr(F\text{ first occurs at }t\mid F\text{ absent before }t),

where λt\lambda_{t} is the marginal hazard, averaged over histories surviving to tt. The path-level hazard λt​(Ht−1)\lambda_{t}(H_{t-1}) may depend on the task, preceding history Ht−1H_{t-1}, and active controls, so the empirical question is how history shapes it.

Several results are consistent with hazards that rise after errors. Closest to an intervention, Sinha et al. supply knowledge and plans, then show that injecting erroneous earlier outputs into history reduces later accuracy (Sinha et al., 2026). In repeated Toolathlon runs, controlling for model and task, an off-canonical call is associated with a 22.7-point increase in next-call deviation (Lee, 2026). SWE-agent’s GPT-4 edits eventually succeed 90.5% of the time, but only 57.2% after a failed edit (Yang et al., 2024). At larger scale, every Vending-Bench model had runs that derailed, and breakdowns did not coincide with context-window filling (Backlund and Petersson, 2025). Across 1,794 coding-agent trajectories, annotated failures were predominantly epistemic, with early onset and late-surfacing symptoms (Zhao et al., 2026). Across 2,518 TRAVERSE trajectories, agents often failed to recover from a first mistake and rarely caught their own errors (Rahman et al., 2026). The injected-history design and a natural experiment holding model and task fixed (Lee, 2026) support causal claims. The rest are observational, and because errors are not randomly assigned, task difficulty may partly explain their associations; in pooled failure-prediction data, almost every pair behind the reported AUROC compares runs of different tasks, and within-task discrimination early in a run is near chance (EsfandyariDoulabi et al., 2026).

A three-state model with illustrative parameters shows why detection and recovery matter. Let states 𝖼,𝗑,𝖿\mathsf{c},\mathsf{x},\mathsf{f} denote clean, contaminated, and irreversibly failed execution, with unit vectors e𝖼,e𝗑e_{\mathsf{c}},e_{\mathsf{x}}:

(4) K=(1−qq0r1−r−bb001),q∈[0,1],r,b≥0,r+b≤1,K=\begin{pmatrix}1-q&q&0\\ r&1-r-b&b\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad q\in[0,1],\ r,b\geq 0,\ r+b\leq 1,

where qq introduces an error, rr recovers, and bb turns contamination into failure. Early, hidden errors correspond to a small detection-driven rr, and meltdown loops to a rarely left contaminated state. With q=.03q=.03 and b=.05b=.05, raising rr from 0 to .25.25 raises survival e𝖼⊤​KN​(e𝖼+e𝗑)e_{\mathsf{c}}^{\top}K^{N}(e_{\mathsf{c}}+e_{\mathsf{x}}) at N=100N=100 from about 0.1 to about 0.6, and the clean endpoint e𝖼⊤​KN​e𝖼e_{\mathsf{c}}^{\top}K^{N}e_{\mathsf{c}} from about 0.05 to about 0.6 (Figure 3). Long-run survival in this model thus depends mainly on the detection-driven recovery rate rr.

B.2. Persistent state and contaminated evidence

This subsection turns to the state an agent carries between steps: context, memory, and stored evidence. Agents can fail to use evidence, not only lose it through truncation, summarization, or cache compression. For example, relevant information placed in the middle of a long prompt can go unused (Liu et al., 2024a), while retrieval and external memory (Lewis et al., 2020; Packer et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023) add further problems of selection, freshness, and retraction. Planning benchmarks show what losing constraints costs. In TravelPlanner, GPT-4 reached a 0.6% final success rate, failing to stay on task, choose tools, and track multiple constraints (Xie et al., 2024a). MemoryAgentBench separately evaluates retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, and selective forgetting, and no evaluated memory design masters all four (Hu et al., 2026b). Stored evidence should therefore keep its source, version, and uncertainty through summarization, because otherwise a summary that turns “not checked” into “verified” silently changes the item’s meaning (Section C.2).

B.3. Actions, trust boundaries, and external impact

This subsection concerns actions, the point where an agent’s decision becomes an effect in a system it does not control. A valid tool call can be the wrong action, so tool-learning benchmarks separate tool-selection errors from invocation errors (Qin et al., 2024). Emulation and injection studies show harmful actions can also be syntactically ordinary (Ruan et al., 2024; Debenedetti et al., 2024). Indirect prompt injection crosses a central boundary between data that informs a decision and authority that permits an effect, along three paths: instructions embedded in retrieved content (Greshake et al., 2023), poisoned memory that persists across sessions, as in AgentPoison (Chen et al., 2024b), and tool ecosystems, where Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers present 16 lifecycle threat scenarios (Hou et al., 2026) and MCP tools can coerce leading models into malicious code execution and credential theft (Halloran et al., 2026). Measured attack success depends on the threat model. InjecAgent reports 24% for its ReAct-prompted GPT-4 setting over 1,054 cases (Zhan et al., 2024), whereas AgentDojo pairs 97 legitimate tasks with 629 security cases (Debenedetti et al., 2024).

Recovery after an action takes effect depends on deployment: a test database can be reset, but a sent message stays sent. Silence is not evidence of failure, because a lost response may follow a successful commit. Retry safety therefore requires execution evidence, deduplication, or reconciliation (Wu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026b). Two 2026 benchmarks measure the cost of getting this wrong: in LIMBO, frontier models duplicate an in-flight or redelivered write in 56–74% of episodes, and an idempotency key on every write lowers the duplicate rate from 28% to 4% (Li, 2026); in UndoBench, naive retry after a lost acknowledgment duplicated external effects in 53% of trials (Sah et al., 2026).

B.4. Verification with incomplete or dependent evidence

This subsection considers what a check can establish when it shares evidence with the work it checks. Verification can target action validity, state fidelity, progress, or completion; a correct final state can coexist with harmful intermediate actions. The central difficulty is that verifiers often share the worker’s information. Intrinsic self-correction can fail to improve or even degrade reasoning (Huang et al., 2024), whereas Self-Refine and chain-of-verification gain when feedback or independent questions are available (Madaan et al., 2023; Dhuliawala et al., 2024). Diagnosing agent traces is itself hard: on the 148 annotated traces of TRAIL (Trace Reasoning and Agentic Issue Localization), the best long-context model scored 11% (Deshpande et al., 2025). Agents also misreport their own checking: coding agents skipped files they were asked to review in 68% of runs and, in 80% of those, claimed a complete review or left the gap undisclosed (Smyth et al., 2026); under injected tool faults, agents flagged an explicit error in 91% of trials but a plausible wrong value in only 59% (Kraishan, 2026). Given shared evidence, verification claims should state what was checked and where, separately from confidence and correctness.

B.5. Coordination and common-cause failure

This subsection looks at errors that arise between agents rather than within one. Multi-agent frameworks distribute work through roles, messages, and shared artifacts (Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024a), which improves decomposition but introduces stale reads, conflicting writes, and unclear ownership. An enforced access rule prevents one agent from overwriting another’s work, although it protects only the operations it covers. Fault injection into inter-agent messages shows how far errors travel: across 29,000 executions, 21% of failures produced no immediate signal, and a flat topology kept 53% task success under message faults where sequential and hierarchical topologies kept about 3%, because an alternative path preserved the evidence (Zhou et al., 2026). Adversarial content in shared artifacts reached 60–80% of agents over up to eight handoffs (Pulipaka et al., 2026), and CaMeL’s per-agent guarantee does not compose when one agent calls another as a tool (Peters-Gill et al., 2026). Classical results also limit coordination: FLP rules out guaranteed deterministic consensus in an asynchronous system with even one crash fault (Fischer et al., 1985), so practical protocols assume partial synchrony (Castro and Liskov, 1999).

B.6. Human oversight and limited attention

The last challenge is the human in the loop. Oversight adds judgment and authority, but its capacity depends on reviewer workload and available evidence. Pan et al.’s study of 86 deployed systems across 26 domains (MAP) found that 68% of systems run at most ten steps before intervention and 74% rely primarily on human evaluation (Pan et al., 2026). READY makes oversight cost measurable: two systems 0.3 points apart in autonomous accuracy required 39.2% versus 29.6% human review to reach the same 76% reliability target (Chatrath et al., 2026). Programming-assistant studies show the same need to measure review effort (Vaithilingam et al., 2022), and in a controlled study of 36 participants overseeing a coding agent, people were confident while missing silent defects, because they ran generic checks rather than generating diagnostic evidence (Dissanayake et al., 2026).

B.7. Seven dynamics

Table 7 consolidates the challenges into seven overlapping dynamics, and the evidence above supports trajectory amplification as a working hypothesis: error rates rise after earlier errors, onset is early while symptoms appear late, and derailment is unrelated to context capacity.

To test whether the framework can express an independently derived taxonomy, Table 8 maps the 14 failure modes of MAST (Cemri et al., 2025) onto it. Every mode maps onto at least one phase–domain cell, and modes that MAST lists separately can share a coordinate. For example, task derailment and reasoning–action mismatch are both P1/R2 deviations from an explicit reference (H3). MAST’s conversational focus excludes model and compute state (R1), external impact (H5), and recovery of committed effects. Eight of the 14 modes have no intrinsic dynamic. For instance, premature termination, a termination-decision error (P4–P6), implies exhaustion when a budget forced the stop, while incorrect verification causes contamination when the accepted output is reused. Section 4.5 tests this mapping empirically. The mapping is our interpretation of MAST’s published definitions.

Appendix C Mechanisms: What They Control and What They Assume

Established reliability methods work precisely where their assumptions hold for the agent, so we compare controls by what each establishes and assumes. Planning and memory support consistent decisions (Sections C.1–C.2), while enforcement, recovery, and verification limit incorrect effects (Sections C.3–C.4), and coordination and oversight govern shared work (Sections C.5–C.6). Section C.7 compares all families and their composition.

C.1. Planning, decomposition, and learned execution

Deliberation and search.

These methods address how agents reason and plan before acting. Chain-of-thought and self-consistency help where intermediate reasoning or sampled answers are informative (Wei et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023), and ReAct couples deliberation to observations (Yao et al., 2023b). ReWOO separates planning from execution and reduces model calls (Xu et al., 2023). Tree of Thoughts and LATS search with evaluation and backtracking (Yao et al., 2023a; Zhou et al., 2024a), while SayCan ties plans to feasible actions (Ahn et al., 2022). LLM-Modulo delegates plan validity to external verifiers (Kambhampati et al., 2024). RAP plans with an LLM world model (Hao et al., 2023). On long tasks, plans go stale, replanning follows faulty observations, search depends on its evaluator, and planning on its model.

Revision, skills, and harness structure.

These methods add revision, retained experience or control structure. Self-Refine revises answers, Reflexion retains episodic feedback, and Voyager accumulates executable skills (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a). A skill with a testable postcondition is a stronger contract than an unverified lesson, because it can be checked. Revision needs discriminating feedback, or iteration can reinforce a wrong diagnosis (Huang et al., 2024). CRITIC grounds revision in tool feedback, and process supervision evaluates intermediate steps (Gou et al., 2024; Lightman et al., 2024). Decomposition with local error detection and voting sustains a million-step task (Meyerson et al., 2025), while fixed workflows such as Agentless show that simpler control can be preferable (Xia et al., 2025). LongHorizon-Harness stores task state outside the model’s context, updates it with environment-verified facts, and reports gains on Terminal-Bench and OSWorld (Ma et al., 2026). This trades a contamination risk in task state (H2, R2) for an environment check (P4, R4) performed before each planning decision.

Training and admission.

These methods train agents for long tasks. WebRL trains web agents with a curriculum built from failed attempts and an outcome reward model (Qi et al., 2025). SWE-RL uses a rule-based similarity reward on software-evolution data (Wei et al., 2025), and AREX combines constraint-wise verification with long-horizon training (Lu et al., 2026). Such rewards can improve completion yet leave unrewarded properties, such as avoiding harmful intermediate actions, to runtime checks. A task contract fixed at admission (P0) records outcome, non-goals, evidence, limits and authority, so acceptance criteria stay unchanged as the plan evolves.

C.2. Memory and compute-state fidelity

This subsection covers controls over what an agent remembers, from the KV cache to external memory. Memory operations differ in what they preserve, so each kind needs its own evaluation (Figure 4).

Exact operations. PagedAttention changes where key–value (KV) cache entries are stored but preserves logical access, and FlashAttention computes exact attention up to floating-point reordering (Kwon et al., 2023; Dao et al., 2022). Divergence beyond floating-point nondeterminism therefore indicates an implementation or numerical fault, not lossy retention. Lossy retention. H2O, Scissorhands, and SnapKV select which positions to retain (Zhang et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023b; Li et al., 2024), whereas KIVI quantizes stored values (Liu et al., 2024c). Their selection signals do not measure a task constraint’s importance, so both approaches should be evaluated by their effect on later decisions under matched budgets. Agent-context compression. ACON refines natural-language compression guidelines from analyses of agent failures. This reduces peak tokens by 26–54% while improving success on AppWorld, OfficeBench, and multi-objective QA (Kang et al., 2026). The result supports judging compression by its effect on later decisions.

External-memory systems each control a different aspect of memory. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies non-parametric evidence (Lewis et al., 2020), while MemGPT manages memory tiers (Packer et al., 2023). Self-RAG and CRAG control retrieval timing and evidence quality (Asai et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2024). Generative Agents, A-MEM, and Mem0 consolidate and link memories (Park et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025b; Chhikara et al., 2025). Stored facts need verification, so we propose two requirements. First, memory should record source versions, observation times, uncertainty, and dependent conclusions, so a changed fact invalidates the conclusions built on it. Second, instructions quoted in stored text should never trigger actions, because quoting an instruction does not authorize it.

For R1, hardware protection and fail-stop assumptions remain relevant (Koren and Krishna, 2007; Schlichting and Schneider, 1983). Fault-injection tools such as Ares and PyTorchFI measure how perturbations affect inference (Reagen et al., 2018; Mahmoud et al., 2020). One study in our corpus follows such perturbations into agent loops: Rubey et al. inject random two-bit weight faults in 4,300 agent runs and find that agents often recover and complete the task, at higher cost, while a few faults produce semantically meaningful errors with otherwise normal behavior (Rubey et al., 2026).

C.3. Interface enforcement and recovery boundaries

This subsection covers controls at the interface between the agent and its environment, before and after an action takes effect. Valid format, permission, and reversibility are independent guarantees. Enforcement constrains an action before it occurs, whereas isolation, rollback, and compensation address its effects afterward.

Pre-execution schemas, policies, and guardrails.

Constrained decoding enforces grammars (Willard and Louf, 2023; Beurer-Kellner et al., 2023), but a valid parse does not prove authorization. AgentSpec evaluates user rules at runtime triggers (Wang et al., 2026a). CaMeL separates trusted control flow from untrusted data and checks capabilities (Debenedetti et al., 2026). Progent checks tool calls against symbolic privilege rules, narrowing automatically but requiring approval to expand (Shi et al., 2025). Llama Guard constrains conversational inputs and outputs (Inan et al., 2023), whereas GuardAgent and ShieldAgent check proposed actions with generated code or policy-derived rule circuits (Xiang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). Instruction Hierarchy trains models to resist injected instructions (Wallace et al., 2024). Deterministic decisions are only as reliable as their rules, learned decisions need their error measured on the deployment distribution, and a check goes stale unless it is bound to the resource version it examined.

Post-execution isolation, restoration, and compensation.

MicroVMs limit reachable resources (Agache et al., 2020), emulated tools avoid real services (Ruan et al., 2024), and checkpoint/restart and message logging restore computational state (Elnozahy et al., 2002). The question is what a snapshot contains and which effects escaped it. Retry, replan, rollback, compensation, and escalation differ in preconditions and residual risks. Retry is safe only with evidence of non-execution, idempotence, or deduplication. Compensation issues an offsetting action, as in sagas (Garcia-Molina and Salem, 1987), and can itself fail. Self-healing designs (Ghosh et al., 2007) also need versions, because a rewound agent can conflict with peers.

Agent-specific recovery runtimes.

Several 2026 works, mostly preprints, show that checkpoint-and-restore can replay or fork externally visible actions unless it records which effects were released. After a restore, an agent may reconstruct a slightly different request that the server treats as new (Figure 5; Table 9 compares the systems). ACRFence names these semantic rollback attacks, including action replay and authority resurrection, and enforces replay-or-fork semantics over recorded irreversible effects (Zheng et al., 2026b). Wu et al. identify five checkpoint-and-rollback failure modes across five frameworks, demonstrating malware-verification bypass, unauthorized mail forwarding, and double payment (Wu et al., 2026). Among constructive systems, Cordon stages outward effects in an outbox and validates the composed flow before release (Chen et al., 2026b). Zheng et al. decide exactly, with mechanized proofs, whether a checkpoint, fork, restore, or merge is safe (Zheng et al., 2026a). AgentRewind checkpoints agent context with a controlled environment (Zhuang et al., 2026), and REVISE recomputes only work invalidated by a revision (Qi et al., 2026). Planarian snapshots local state and records compensating actions for remote changes, which rollback replays (Guo et al., 2026), and a commit-time authority service rejects stale proposals and dispatches effects through an idempotent outbox (Salas, 2026). Recovery can also harm: the same intervention rescues some trajectories and disrupts others, so a router that decides when to intervene raises success (Xiao et al., 2026). All still depend on provider semantics for released effects.

C.4. Verification: tests, monitors, and model judges

This subsection covers the checks that decide whether work is acceptable: tests, monitors, and model judges. Runtime verification checks properties against execution events (Leucker and Schallhart, 2009), so its verdicts cover only those properties and events. Software tasks offer tests (Jimenez et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), but suites differ in coverage, and stronger tests change which solutions pass (Liu et al., 2023a). WebArena, AppWorld, and τ\tau-bench check environment state (Zhou et al., 2024b; Trivedi et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025) with privileges deployments may lack, so a benchmark oracle is not a runtime verifier.

Model judges assess semantic requirements, and chain-of-verification, debate, and multi-judge systems organize this checking differently (Dhuliawala et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2024). MT-Bench and FairEval document judge biases, including sensitivity to answer order (Zheng et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024b). Agent-as-a-Judge inspects intermediate artifacts. On 55 development tasks it outperformed LLM-as-a-Judge and matched the reliability of its human-evaluation baseline (Zhuge et al., 2025). Let WW denote a wrong worker output and VV acceptance, so false acceptance has probability Pr⁡(W)​Pr⁡(V∣W)\Pr(W)\Pr(V\mid W). The conditional rate Pr⁡(V∣W)\Pr(V\mid W) records how often the verifier accepts the worker’s actual errors. It should be measured because overall accuracy can hide a high value. Deferral thresholds likewise need calibration on the agent’s outputs (Guo et al., 2017). A judge adds most value when it reads evidence the worker did not use. A different-model judge helps only if its errors differ from the worker’s; error overlap should be measured directly (Figure 6). For approval monitors, every reliable fooling in one study came through a shared evidence source, so counting independent sources rather than votes blocked 0.9% of correct payments against 7.4% for the best vote-counting rule at equal safety (Zanolini, 2026).

C.5. Coordination protocols and redundancy

This subsection covers how shared work among agents is organized and when redundancy helps. Belief–desire–intention (BDI) models, blackboards, and protocols organize shared work (Wooldridge, 2009; Rao and Georgeff, 1995), whereas LLM frameworks use role-based pipelines, multi-agent conversations, and state machines (Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024a; Wu et al., 2024b). For example, HuggingGPT and LLMCompiler dispatch specialized models or parallel calls (Shen et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024). Role names do not supply dependability, which requires enforced ownership, versioned handoffs, restricted writes, and bounded termination. Self-consistency, debate, and mixtures of agents aid candidate selection (Wang et al., 2023; Du et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a), but, like N-version programming and recovery blocks (Avižienis, 1985; Randell, 1975; Lyu, 1995), they depend on diversity, because replicas of one model tend to share errors. Agreement protocols (Schneider, 1990; Castro and Liskov, 1999) make replicas agree but not correct, a limit that majority voting among agents shares.

C.6. Observability, human review, and audit

This subsection covers the records and human processes that support review during and after a run. Records serve three purposes: tracing, review, and audit. Distributed tracing links events through causal context (Sigelman et al., 2010), but agents also need semantic links, such as links from sources to claims and from approvals to effects. Who&When, AgentRx, LongRCA, and TRAIL localize responsible agents, steps, and error types (Zhang et al., 2025b; Barke et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Deshpande et al., 2025). Dependency-guided attribution outperforms chronology-based judges on Who&When (Deng et al., 2026a), and BRIDGE compiles handoff traces into a provenance graph to repair broken handoffs at run time (Su et al., 2026). The Agent Error Dataset pairs 50,000 failures with replay-checked diagnoses (Zhu et al., 2026), while an audit of attribution benchmarks finds surface cues that let simple predictors match GPT-4.1 (Xu and Gao, 2026). Review packets should therefore expose proposed effects, checks, uncertainty, and required decisions. READY selects the minimum-cost oversight policy meeting a reliability target and qualifies it statistically (Chatrath et al., 2026), LEASH escalates from a weak to a strong computer-use agent when step-level uncertainty rises (Wang et al., 2026c), while cognitive-forcing experiments show that interface design changes overreliance (Buçinca et al., 2021). Model cards and datasheets are precedents for agent records (Mitchell et al., 2019; Gebru et al., 2021), and such records need maintenance as systems change (Sculley et al., 2015).

C.7. Composition: align control and effect boundaries

Combining controls is safe only if the state each component checks is the state the next uses. We represent a control by (Ai,Gi,Ωi,ℬi)(A_{i},G_{i},\Omega_{i},\mathcal{B}_{i}): assumptions, guarantee, observable state, and enforcement or restoration boundary. In Table 10, AiA_{i}, Ωi\Omega_{i}, and ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i} correspond to the columns principal assumptions, inspection basis, and enforces or restores. The protects column names the state domain that GiG_{i} is about, whereas GiG_{i} itself is a property of that state. A test gate, for example, protects the repository (R4), and its guarantee is that commit vv passes test suite TT; a release step that follows assumes that the artifact it deploys is vv. Cost and residual risk are not part of the contract. For consecutive deterministic controls under environment assumptions Γ\Gamma, a sufficient compatibility obligation is

(5) Γ∧Gi⊧Ai+1.\Gamma\land G_{i}\ \models\ A_{i+1}.

A gap can remain between check and commit, for example between tested version vv and release v+1v+1, or approved arguments aa and rewritten a′a^{\prime}. Where supported, version binding or atomic compare-and-update closes this gap.

For two probabilistic checks with miss events M1M_{1} and M2M_{2}, the joint miss probability is Pr⁡(M1)​Pr⁡(M2∣M1)\Pr(M_{1})\Pr(M_{2}\mid M_{1}). The second check’s value therefore depends on its miss rate on the first check’s misses, not its marginal accuracy. Checks reading the same inputs can be expected to have Pr⁡(M2∣M1)\Pr(M_{2}\mid M_{1}) well above Pr⁡(M2)\Pr(M_{2}), so this dependence should be measured rather than assumed.

Recovery must also leave every running component consistent; restoring a database while a client keeps its old view violates this. Table 10 compares the control families of Sections C.1–C.6 along six dimensions.

Choosing among controls.

The choice of control should follow the error’s boundary. Hazards expressible as predicates over actions or information flow suit deterministic enforcement, which holds by construction within its mediation; semantic hazards suit learned guards whose false-acceptance rate is measurable on the deployment distribution. Where effects can be deferred, staging removes the need to undo them. For effects that cannot be deferred, the remaining defenses are effect logs with replay-or-fork and provider-side idempotence, since snapshot restore alone suffices only for snapshot-capable state. Where an executable oracle exists, tests dominate model judges for the requirements they cover; elsewhere, judges help only when they read evidence the worker did not use, and redundancy only when error diversity is shown.

Appendix D Evaluation: Outcomes, Episodes, and Causal Claims

The value of a benchmark score depends on what the test observes and which runs it includes, so task cohorts, failure-conditioned corpora and constructed stress tests support different claims even with the same model and environment (Figure 7). We compare task benchmarks (Section D.1) with adversarial and diagnostic studies (Section D.2) and propose measurements and designs (Sections D.3–D.5).

D.1. Task benchmarks and their observability

SWE-bench and SWE-Bench Pro test repository-scale correctness via versioned tasks and executable tests (Jimenez et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2026b), so results depend on test adequacy, environment setup, and release version. WebArena, OSWorld, and AppWorld expose web, desktop, and API actions with functional or state-based evaluators (Zhou et al., 2024b; Xie et al., 2024b; Trivedi et al., 2024), whereas Mind2Web’s offline task measures reproduction of demonstrated actions (Deng et al., 2023). Further benchmarks add visual grounding, enterprise software, mobile, conversational navigation, and lengthy open-web tasks (Koh et al., 2024; Drouin et al., 2024; Rawles et al., 2025; Lù et al., 2024; Yoran et al., 2024). Others cover heterogeneous environments, progress, API use, and tool-supported answers (Liu et al., 2024b; Ma et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2024; Mialon et al., 2024), with BrowserGym unifying evaluation (De Chezelles et al., 2025). τ\tau-bench scores database state under policies with simulated users (Yao et al., 2025). In τ2\tau^{2}-bench, agent and user both act on shared state, so evaluation must check its consistency (Barres et al., 2026).

Newer benchmarks target consequential, long-running work: a simulated software company (Xu et al., 2025a), Kaggle competitions (Chan et al., 2025), priced freelance tasks (Miserendino et al., 2025), hard command-line tasks (Merrill et al., 2026), and 20-million-token business simulations (Backlund and Petersson, 2025). RE-Bench, comparing agents with eight-hour expert attempts (Wijk et al., 2025), shows that budget length decides who looks stronger. Agents scored four times higher than humans at two hours; humans scored twice as high at 32 total hours. Because these benchmarks stress different components of the horizon (Section 2.2) and measure horizon differently, their scores share no single horizon scale.

D.2. Adversarial, long-horizon, and diagnostic evidence

Security benchmarks each define an attacker surface and threat model. AgentDojo pairs legitimate tasks with injections, while InjecAgent injects malicious tool content (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Zhan et al., 2024). Agent Security Bench broadens attack and defense settings, whereas AgentHarm tests explicitly harmful requests (Zhang et al., 2025a; Andriushchenko et al., 2025). Indirect hijacking and deliberate misuse are distinct threats, so report their rates separately. Long-horizon stress tests reach hundreds of tool calls or thousands of trajectories (Luo et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026d). Recovery now has benchmarks of its own: CUA-Recovery places agents in 2,250 verified erroneous desktop states, where error awareness reaches at most 44% (Hu et al., 2026a); ReTrace judges a recovery by whether downstream actions yield the same outcomes as from the target state (Bang et al., 2026); and UndoBench and LIMBO score recovery against ledgers of committed effects (Sah et al., 2026; Li, 2026). Memory benchmarks isolate temporal reasoning, updates, abstention, and selective forgetting (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026b).

Failure-attribution corpora identify which role or step explains a failed run (Zhang et al., 2025b; Deshpande et al., 2025; Barke et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). Step-level diagnosis is far harder. The best Who&When method found the responsible agent 53.5% of the time, but the decisive step only 14.2%. In LongRCA, root causes lie a median 48 steps before run end, and the strongest baseline reached 13.2% exact root-step accuracy. TRAVERSE adds 2,518 human-annotated trajectories, yet the best of six frontier judges found the first mistake in under a third of runs (Rahman et al., 2026). These corpora assess diagnosis of known failures only, not failure frequency or whether one root step exists, and their labels have their own uncertainty: MAST’s κ=0.88\kappa=0.88 was measured by three annotators on 15 of its 150 development traces, and its 1,642-trace dataset is labeled by an LLM judge (Cemri et al., 2025). Role accuracy, step accuracy, and repair usefulness therefore need separate reporting (Wang et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2026a).

D.3. A minimal measurement protocol

Trajectory-level claims need a minimal record so that outcome changes can be attributed to the right harness change: task, trial, versions, budget, realized horizon, disposition, and harness configuration (model, prompts, tools, memory, verifier, recovery policy, human boundary).

Repeated-trial reliability needs care because common metrics answer different questions. Pass@kk asks whether at least one of kk trials succeeds, whereas passk\mathrm{pass}^{k}, introduced in τ\tau-bench (Yao et al., 2025), asks whether all kk succeed. For nn reset trials with cc successes, and assuming exchangeable trials (valid when earlier attempts leave external state unchanged for later trials),

(6) pass​@​k^=1−(n−ck)(nk),passk^=(ck)(nk),k≤n.\widehat{\mathrm{pass@}k}=1-\frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}},\qquad\widehat{\mathrm{pass}^{k}}=\frac{\binom{c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}},\quad k\leq n.

Verifier coverage also needs a denominator, which is the set of applicable requirement–event obligations 𝒪⁡(τ)\mathcal{O}(\tau) with checking deadlines:

(7) Cov(τ)=|{o∈𝒪⁡(τ):the required check ran before its deadline}||𝒪⁡(τ)|.\operatorname{Cov}(\tau)=\frac{|\{o\in\mathcal{O}(\tau):\text{the required check ran before its deadline}\}|}{|\mathcal{O}(\tau)|}.

It counts executed checks, not their soundness. Reporting it by requirement type prevents repeated easy checks from hiding an untested one. Cost per success, ∑iCi/∑iYi\sum_{i}C_{i}/\sum_{i}Y_{i}, must include failed attempts, recovery, and review effort (Chatrath et al., 2026).

D.4. Experimental designs that isolate a mechanism

Three designs each change one preset property while keeping the task goal fixed. The first two vary horizon and dependency structure, so the compared tasks must match on everything except duration or dependency distance. The third studies error propagation and containment. A dependency-delay intervention varies the steps between observing a fact and using it, crossed with the summarization policy; a repeated-operation intervention adds validated operations whose postconditions are known; and a state intervention injects a false premise, stale response, omitted message, or numerical perturbation at a declared phase and domain, which tests containment under that injection. Each design should randomize at task or trial level, retain clean controls, include successful and failed runs, and compare at a fixed budget and at equal task success. Crossing two controls factorially estimates their interaction, which tests whether aligned controls reduce escaping errors.

D.5. Statistical reporting

Estimate uncertainty by treating tasks as clusters, because steps correlate, and audit a subset of model-judged outcomes for false acceptance and rejection. Under a fixed budget, count every attempted task and distinguish completion, policy failure, escalation, and timeout. For time-to-failure estimates, treat successful completion as a competing terminal event and report cumulative incidence; only stops unrelated to failure risk, such as a budget cutoff, count as censored. Combining failure-enriched corpora with representative runs requires a sampling model and weights, while stratifying by realized length requires addressing errors that lengthen runs.

Appendix E Published Evidence and Research Priorities

E.1. Findings supported by published results

We grade each finding’s evidence: strong by construction if it rests on a demonstrated mechanism or a design guarantee, moderate if consistent but observational or setting-specific, and descriptive if it concerns research attention rather than system behavior. F1–F3 concern where errors enter and spread, F4–F6 which controls interrupt them, and F7 and OP1–OP5 what evaluations establish.

  • •

    F1. Errors make later errors more likely (moderate). In coding, tool-use, and controlled reasoning tasks, error rates after an error exceed baseline, and failure onset tends to precede symptoms by many steps (Sinha et al., 2026; Lee, 2026; Yang et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2026; Rahman et al., 2026). A history-dependent hazard (Equation 3) is therefore a better starting model than independent steps. Outside injected-history and natural-experiment designs, part of the effect may reflect task difficulty.

  • •

    F2. Length alone does not explain reliability (moderate). Decomposition with local error control sustained a million-step task. Vending-Bench derailment decouples from context saturation, and the RE-Bench human–agent ranking reverses with the time budget (Meyerson et al., 2025; Backlund and Petersson, 2025; Wijk et al., 2025). Claims about “long-horizon failure” should therefore name the changed horizon component and dependency structure.

  • •

    F3. Losing evidence and failing to use it are different faults (moderate). Long-context studies show evidence present but unused, and planning agents leave gathered constraints unused (Liu et al., 2024a; Xie et al., 2024a). Memory and compression studies instead show evidence lost before use (Hu et al., 2026b). Compression should thus be judged by its effect on later decisions (Kang et al., 2026).

  • •

    F4. For indirect prompt injection, data–authority separation is a central security boundary (strong by construction). Attacks through content, memory, or tool metadata succeed when data gains the power to trigger actions (Greshake et al., 2023; Debenedetti et al., 2024; Hou et al., 2026). Architectural separation with deterministic privilege control blocks these attacks by design when the policy is correct and covers the relevant operations (Debenedetti et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2025), a guarantee different in kind from the probabilistic robustness of trained defenses, although it does not compose across agents that call one another (Peters-Gill et al., 2026). The utility cost is measurable: on AgentDojo, CaMeL completes 77% of tasks against 84% without a defense (Debenedetti et al., 2026).

  • •

    F5. Local checkpointing alone does not make retry of external actions safe (strong by construction; defenses are recent preprints). Restored agents re-issue already committed actions, including payments (Wu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026b), and recovery benchmarks measure duplicate effects in half or more of naive retries (Li, 2026; Sah et al., 2026). Safe recovery needs a record of released effects and an explicit restoration boundary (Chen et al., 2026b; Zheng et al., 2026a).

  • •

    F6. Agreement is weak evidence when evidence is shared (moderate). Self-correction can degrade reasoning, judges show position bias, and on TRAIL the best model localizes only 11% of trace errors (Huang et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024b; Deshpande et al., 2025). Gains appear when tests or inspected artifacts supply new evidence (Zhuge et al., 2025). A verifier therefore adds value through independent evidence or measured error diversity, and approval rules should count independent sources rather than votes (Zanolini, 2026).

  • •

    F7. Benchmark success and deployability differ (moderate). Repeated-trial reliability falls far below single-trial success. On τ\tau-bench retail, pass8\mathrm{pass}^{8} was below 25% for a model succeeding on under half of tasks (Yao et al., 2025). Final-state checks miss collateral changes unless they test for them, as AppWorld does (Trivedi et al., 2024), so runs scored as solved can still delete data (Rahman et al., 2026). Equal accuracy can demand very different amounts of human review (Chatrath et al., 2026).

E.2. Illustrative case analysis: what an episode record adds

We test the framework on two published failure traces: the running example from TheAgentCompany (Xu et al., 2025a) and a multi-agent trace that MAST publishes with human annotations (Appendix N.8 of (Cemri et al., 2025)). We classify each failure with the symptom label given by its source, with Ding et al.’s state-centered axes (Ding et al., 2026), and with the episode record (Equation 1). The facts come from the released trajectories; the classification and the indicated controls are ours (Table 11).

Case A: a shortcut that changes the environment, then a wait that never ends.

The trace is the released trajectory of the Amazon Nova Pro run on the benchmark’s example task (Xu et al., 2025a), introduced in Section 1; the paper describes the pattern as renaming another user, and the released trace shows the agent renaming its own administrator account. The agent, logged into the company chat as an administrator, is to obtain a repository location from a colleague, Alex Turner, clone the repository, and start a server. Its second browser action opens the user administration page, and seven actions later it has set the name and username of its own account to “Alex Turner”, so the directory lists two users of that name. After a guessed repository URL, a guessed wiki URL, and two web searches fail, it opens a direct message with a different colleague, Mike Chen, and writes “Hi Alex, could you please provide me with the repository URL”. From then on it answers every prompt to continue by saying that it is waiting for Alex Turner, 81 times, until the run ends after 22 minutes without a finish action. The benchmark’s authors report this pattern as a fabricated shortcut; the state-centered axes flag an identity record changed without authority. The episode record adds the chain (Table 11). As Section 2.4 recorded, the origin is a P1 decision in R2 to alter the directory rather than search it; the P2 action mutates R4 and R6, so an identity in a shared system points at the agent itself; the wrong-recipient message (R5) contaminates the R2 belief at P3 (H2); the directory listing and the message header displayed the evidence, but no P4 check read them, and no P5 response or P6 escalation followed before the budget ran out (H7). Three controls are indicated: a P0 scope rule that excludes directory writes from a task that only reads it, a P2 recipient check against the conversation partner, and a P5 stall rule that escalates after a bounded number of identical waiting turns. A local checkpoint would address none of these, because restoring the agent’s state leaves the renamed account in place (F5).

Case B: an example output accepted as a test result.

HyperAgent, a planner–navigator–executor system, works on a Matplotlib issue from SWE-bench Lite in which a RangeSlider callback blocks input to other widgets. The released trace runs through seven planner rounds and six sub-agent handoffs (four navigator, one editor, one executor) with 23 inner tool steps; the executor’s report is the last handoff. After the planner’s change, the executor writes and runs a test script. The script opens an interactive window, so its only output is a font-cache message. The executor notes that the plot must be operated by hand. Even so, its report to the planner lists interaction steps and concludes that the blocking issue “has been resolved”. The report ends: “The above output is just an example”. The planner replies “Thank you for running the test and providing the results”, states that the solution “has been tested”, and ends the task (Cemri et al., 2025). MAST labels the trace disobey role specification (1.2) and information withholding (2.4), which describe the navigator’s and executor’s behavior. The state-centered axes flag a stored claim without provenance. The episode record shows where the evidence changed status. An R4 observation (the font-cache message) and the executor’s hypothetical output enter the R5 handoff together. The qualifier does not survive the planner’s P3 integration. P4 acceptance and P6 termination therefore rest on example output. In terms of Equation 7, the trace shows no completed interactive test, yet the run recorded the check as passed. The indicated control binds every “tested” claim to an execution record that the planner reads directly; for a GUI fix, the record includes an interaction log or widget-level assertions, not only terminal output. It also blocks termination while a required check is unexecuted. The case also reveals a measurement gap. An end-state score records whether the final patch passes hidden tests, not whether the agent’s own verification took place.

The three framings complement one another. A symptom taxonomy is cheap and supports prevalence counts, and a state-centered analysis identifies which items need governance. The episode record needs event order, message provenance, and execution records; in return, it separates failures that share a label but require different controls.

E.3. Costs and interference

Controls add cost and new failure paths: search and voting use compute, provenance uses storage, approval uses attention, compression can lose a constraint, conservative checks can reject legitimate actions, and staging adds latency (Chen et al., 2026b). Claiming reward hacking requires evidence that optimization raises acceptance without improving independent correctness (Liu et al., 2023a). Trace-length effects on quality remain unmeasured despite widespread review (Pan et al., 2026), so compliant completion, unrecovered impact, latency, compute, and human effort should be reported together.

E.4. Scope and limitations of the background

The findings above rest on published results and inherit their limits: most benchmarks publish end states rather than intermediate state, message provenance, or execution records, so propagation is rarely observable; our labels for what a method restores or contains follow the authors’ descriptions; many reported measurements lack the denominators needed to relate them to a population of runs, which is why findings are graded rather than pooled; and software and question-answering tasks supply most of the evidence. Section 4 addresses the first of these limits directly by annotating released trajectories.

E.5. Five research priorities

Each priority addresses a caveat in Section E.1 or a gap in Section 4 and names a comparison that would settle it (Figure 8).

OP1: Supported propagation graphs. Exact step-level attribution reaches 14.2% on Who&When and 24.1% on LongRCA (Zhang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026). Dependency-guided attribution already improves on chronology-based judges (Deng et al., 2026a), but attribution benchmarks contain surface cues that simple predictors exploit (Xu and Gao, 2026), so comparisons should use held-out tasks, keep natural and injected failures separate, and report cue-control tests.

OP2: Semantic memory and compute state under constrained resources. Exact execution, approximate caches, summarization, learned compression, and external memory should be compared on fixed tasks at equal memory and latency, measuring decision fidelity and retraction. Injecting weight, cache, or computation faults and tracing them through decisions would close the R1 gap.

OP3: Verifier portfolios with measurable blind spots. Seeded violations of action, evidence, progress, and outcome requirements would let tests, policy monitors, guards, judges, fresh retrieval, and humans be compared on common outputs, with source sharing varied separately from model identity so that its effect on joint misses, false rejection, and cost can be measured.

OP4: Recovery across uncertain commitment. Benchmarks should inject timeouts before and after commitment, re-synthesized retries, and compensation failures, so that retry, checkpointing, staging, and reconciliation can be compared by post-recovery consistency and residual impact.

OP5: Horizon interventions with valid stopping rules. Varying dependency delay, repetition, or delegation on matched tasks with fixed harnesses would identify which structural demands change risk, rather than a step limit.

E.6. Implications for research and practice

Table 12 reverses Table 10: it starts from what a deployment does and lists the controls and evidence to demand. Benchmark authors should publish evaluator versions, score populations, and horizon profiles; reviewers should separate model gains from changes in harness, budget, or task selection.
